english.html: ther endure, and patiently suffer all the calamities of the world, and were it death, before consenting to the least thing evil and forbidden by his Lord God <sup class="mk" data-key="q">q</sup>. Moreover, it is greatly to be imputed to the priest or monk who, trusting too much in himself, and not recognising the frailty of his flesh, has too easily and rashly thrust himself forward to make such a vow. Thus, if he stumbles and does not keep it, but soils his body by adultery, so far is he from deserving to be excused from the penalty, that he is in my opinion more reprehensible and punishable than another, as having failed more grievously and doubly: namely by rashness, and by contravention and disobedience to the commandment of God, who forbids all pollution and lechery, singularly adultery <sup class="mk" data-key="r">r</sup>, which he wills to be (as we have already often said) punished with death <sup class="mk" data-key="ſ">ſ</sup>; unless the circumstances should lighten the penalty somewhat, or remit it altogether: as ignorance might well do <sup class="mk" data-key="t">t</sup>, force <sup class="mk" data-key="u">u</sup>, the tenderness of a young age, drawn on by continual lascivious and immodest acts <sup class="mk" data-key="x">x</sup>. And so of other like cases, left to the discretion of a good, holy and equitable judge <sup class="mk" data-key="y">y</sup>.

english.html: Those who give themselves up as prey to the immodest love of women let themselves be so consumed and overcome, little by little, by this mad passion that they sometimes lose their senses by it; and being unable to make a breach in the honour of the woman they pursue, in order to satisfy the lasciviousness of their unbridled desires and disordered appetites, they use a thousand blandishments, wiles and deceptions, nay often have recourse to force — whence is contracted the crime which we call Rape [rapt: in the law of the time, abduction as well as rape], and of which our gallant du Tilh remains sufficiently attainted and convicted. This Rape had been committed upon a married woman, and was therefore undoubtedly worthy of death a. For a woman is ravished not only

notes.citation: Digest 48.6 (Ad legem Iuliam de vi publica), l. Qui coetu, the last paragraph (D. 48.6.5.2, Marcian); Code 9.13 (De raptu virginum, seu viduarum, nec non sanctimonialium), the sole law (C. 9.13.1, Justinian)
notes.original: l. qui cœtu P. fi, D. de vi pub. l. vn. C. de rapt. virg.
notes.gloss: D. 48.6.5.2: he who carries off a woman, unmarried or married, is punished with the ultimate penalty — qui vacantem mulierem rapuit vel nuptam, ultimo supplicio punitur. C. 9.13.1 makes rape capital. The print's fi, is fin., the last paragraph; see the report on the `⟨alt⟩`.

readings.reason: auoit eſté commis is a finite clause after the full stop (iceluy Rapt auoit eſté commis … & par ainſi digne de mort, with eſtoit understood); the infinitive would hang awkwardly from conuaincu; the English is the same either way.
xxxiiij: Causa 34 q. 1 (the wife who takes another husband in error) fits the point on ignorance; Causa 33 q. 1 is on impotence; an inference, flagged for review
fœdiſſimam, the Latin spelling of C. 9.9.20 (Foedissimam earum nequitiam); æ is a wrong ligature
fi, = fin., the last paragraph of l. Qui coetu (D. 48.6.5.2, the one on carrying off a married woman); no paragraph of that law begins Si.
